\section[\ar{الأحد} \ar{الإثنين} \ar{الثلاثاء} \ar{الأربعاء} \ar{الخميس}]{\ar{الأحد} to \ar{الخميس} (al-aḥad to al-khamīs) — Sunday to Thursday, by the numbers}

\label{lesson:AR-C08-al-ahad-al-khamis}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Every language so far in this course names its weekdays for planet-gods. Arabic does something completely different: it just \textbf{counts} them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — The pattern: definite article + ordinal number}]
Five of Arabic's seven days are simply \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}the {[}number{]}th\textquotedblright{}} — the definite article \textbf{\ar{ال}} (\emph{al-}) plus an ordinal built on the number word:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{literally} & \textbf{from the number} & \textbf{day} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{الأحد}} (\emph{al-aḥad}) & \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{first}\textquotedblright{} & \emph{wāḥid}, \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} & Sunday \\
\textbf{\ar{الإثنين}} (\emph{al-ithnayn}) & \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{second}\textquotedblright{} (lit. \textquotedblleft{}the two\textquotedblright{}) & \emph{ithnān}, \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} & Monday \\
\textbf{\ar{الثلاثاء}} (\emph{ath-thulāthāʾ}) & \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{third}\textquotedblright{} & \emph{thalātha}, \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{} & Tuesday \\
\textbf{\ar{الأربعاء}} (\emph{al-arbiʿāʾ}) & \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{fourth}\textquotedblright{} & \emph{arbaʿa}, \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{} & Wednesday \\
\textbf{\ar{الخميس}} (\emph{al-khamīs}) & \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{fifth}\textquotedblright{} & \emph{khamsa}, \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} & Thursday \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No moon, no war-god, no planets at all — just \textbf{day one, day two, day three…} This also tells you something about the week itself: counting starts from \textbf{Sunday}, so Sunday is \textquotedblleft{}day one\textquotedblright{} — the Arabic week, like the Jewish and much of the Christian calendar tradition, begins where the European Monday-first convention doesn't.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}al-aḥad\textquotedblright{} — the first, Sunday{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: count up — \textquotedblleft{}al-ithnayn, ath-thulāthāʾ, al-arbiʿāʾ, al-khamīs\textquotedblright{} — second through fifth{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: contrast — no planet-gods here, just numbers{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} How does Arabic name Sunday through Thursday? (\textbf{As ordinal numbers} — \textquotedblleft{}the first\textquotedblright{} through \textquotedblleft{}the fifth,\textquotedblright{} not planet-gods.) Which number is Sunday, and what does that tell you about the week? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}The first\textquotedblright{}} — the Arabic week counts starting from \textbf{Sunday}.) What Arabic prefix turns a number into \textquotedblleft{}the {[}x{]}th day\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ar{ال}} \emph{al-}, the definite article.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{الجمعة} \ar{السبت}]{\ar{الجمعة} and \ar{السبت} (al-jumʿa, as-sabt) — Friday and Saturday}

\label{lesson:AR-C08-al-jumua-as-sabt}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Five days counted off — and then two days important enough to get \textbf{real names} instead of numbers.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The two named days}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{الجمعة}} (\emph{al-jumʿa}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the gathering},\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{\ar{جمع}} (\emph{jamaʿa}), \textquotedblleft{}to gather, collect.\textquotedblright{} This is the day of the congregational Friday prayer (\emph{ṣalāt al-jumʿa}) — the most religiously significant day of the Islamic week, and important enough to earn its own name rather than a number.
  \item \textbf{\ar{السبت}} (\emph{as-sabt}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Sabbath}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest about how \ar{السبت} differs from Latin's Sabbatum}
You may remember Latin borrowed the word \textbf{Sabbatum} from Hebrew to replace its own pagan \emph{diēs Saturnī} — a loanword crossing from a Semitic language into an Italic one. Arabic's \textbf{\ar{سبت}} (\emph{sabt}) is a different kind of relationship entirely: Arabic \textbf{is itself a Semitic language}, in the same family as Hebrew. So \textbf{as-sabt and Hebrew shabbāt aren't borrower-and-lender — they're cousins}, both descending from the same ancient Semitic root \textbf{\ar{س}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ت}} meaning \textquotedblleft{}to rest, to cease.\textquotedblright{} Where Latin \textbf{borrowed} a foreign word, Arabic simply \textbf{inherited} a family word.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}al-jumʿa\textquotedblright{} — the gathering, Friday{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}as-sabt\textquotedblright{} — the Sabbath, Saturday{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the contrast — Latin borrowed \textquotedblleft{}Sabbatum\textquotedblright{}; Arabic's \textquotedblleft{}sabt\textquotedblright{} is a blood relative of Hebrew \textquotedblleft{}shabbāt\textquotedblright{}{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Why does \textbf{\ar{الجمعة}} break the counting pattern? (\textbf{It's named for the congregational Friday prayer} — \textquotedblleft{}the gathering\textquotedblright{} — not counted as a number.) How is Arabic's \textbf{\ar{السبت}} different from Latin's borrowed \textbf{Sabbatum}? (\textbf{Arabic and Hebrew are both Semitic languages} — \emph{as-sabt} and \emph{shabbāt} are \textbf{cousins} from a shared root, not a loanword crossing between unrelated language families.)
\end{tcolorbox}
